physical_harm: Injuries and marks of injuries on the neck, bleeding from nose and mouth
number_of_offences: Five counts of murder and robbery were charged and upheld
motive: Robbery was alleged as motive, but it was unsubstantiated
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court did not accept the prosecution's reliance on circumstantial evidence, including the testimony of the child witness, fingerprint report, FSL report, and recovery of items. It held that the prosecution failed to establish the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of the child witness PW-8 as unreliable due to lack of corroboration and inconsistencies in her testimony. The court emphasized the need for corroboration of child witness testimony and found PW-8's evidence insufficient.

legal_representation.accused: S. Nagamuthu, Sr. Advocate, Himanshu Agarwal, Ms. Ankita S., Ayush Raj Singh, Veerapan P. and Ms. Pyoli
legal_representation.state: Atul Jha, Sandeep Jha and Dharmendra Kumar Sinha

procedural_irregularity: Unexplained delay in reporting the crime, best evidence withheld, unreliable recovery evidence, uncorroborated child witness testimony

appeal_history.supreme_court: Allowed the appeals, set aside the High Court and Sessions Court judgments, acquitted the appellants

prosecution_argument: The prosecution relied on the testimony of child witness PW-8, recoveries made under Section 27 of the Evidence Act, fingerprint report, FSL report, and the motive of committing robbery. The prosecution argued that the accused were last seen together with the victims and that the recovered items (motorcycle, silver-patti, cash) supported the robbery and murder charges.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution's case was based on uncorroborated testimony of PW-8, unreliable recovery evidence, and unexplained delays in reporting the crime. They also highlighted the lack of identification of recovered items, inconsistencies in witness statements, and the absence of expert examination of forensic evidence.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the burden of proof squarely rests on the prosecution and that there can be no conviction based on surmises, conjectures, or suspicion. It emphasized that the courts must adopt the view favorable to the accused when two views are possible, especially in cases based on circumstantial evidence.
precedent_relied_upon: Jaharlal Das v. State of Orissa (1991) 3 SCC 27; Varkey Joseph v. State of Kerala 1993 Suppl (3) SCC 745; Sujit Biswas v. State of Assam (2013) 12 SCC 406; Kali Ram v. State of Himachal Pradesh (1973) 2 SCC 808; Arjun Marik & Ors. v. State of Bihar 1994 Supp (2) SCC 372; Kanhaiya Lal v. State of Rajasthan (2014) 4 SCC 715
